name: InfoBento
description: MagSafe-mounted dual-eInk companion display that lives on the back of your iPhone. Clamshell with two 2.9-inch 128x296 1-bit displays back-to-back: D (outer) shows real-time data when phone-mounted, P (inner) shows ambient content when standing on a counter. 180-degree hinge, solar charging, $30 target, Kickstarter launch. ~7.2mm folded.

artifacts.name: Device Owner
artifacts.description: Individual who owns an InfoBento display — mounts it on their iPhone via MagSafe or stands it on a counter
responsibilities: Configure bento boxes via web UI
Mount on phone or stand on counter near window
Keep phone paired for BLE sync
Transition device between phone-mounted and counter-standing modes

artifacts.name: Gifter
artifacts.description: Person who purchases and pre-configures an InfoBento as a gift for someone else
responsibilities: Configure initial bento layout for recipient
Pair device to recipients phone or hand off config

artifacts.name: Daily Glancer
artifacts.description: Busy professional who wants a passive, zero-interaction display of key daily info — weather, next event, motivational quote — visible at a glance without unlocking their phone. The founder is this user.
goals: See todays weather and schedule without unlocking phone
Reduce screen time by offloading ambient info to a passive display
Customize what info matters most to them
Peek at the back of the phone to decide if an unlock is worth it
frustrations: Checking phone for simple info leads to distraction rabbit holes
Smart home displays are too expensive and power-hungry
Existing e-paper gadgets are not customizable
Every phone interaction is an attention trap — even a quick weather check becomes 10 minutes of scrolling

artifacts.name: Desk Decorator
artifacts.description: Person who values aesthetic, minimal desk or counter accessories and wants a small display that shows a rotating quote, countdown to vacation, or personal QR code — standing on its own with the solar panel as kickstand
goals: Have a visually pleasing desk or counter accessory that is also functional
Display a personal link or QR code for networking
A device that charges itself near a window without any cables
frustrations: Digital photo frames are too large and power-hungry
Sticky notes with countdowns look unprofessional
No small, elegant way to display a personal QR code
Desk gadgets always need cables or batteries

artifacts.name: Gift Giver
artifacts.description: Someone who wants to give a thoughtful, personalized tech gift that is useful without being overwhelming
goals: Give a unique gift that feels personal and curated
Pre-configure the device so the recipient can use it immediately
Gift something that does not require technical knowledge to enjoy
frustrations: Most tech gifts require complex setup
Subscription-based gifts feel like an obligation

artifacts.name: Zero Device Interaction
artifacts.statement: The InfoBento itself requires no interaction — no buttons, no app to open, no charging ritual. You interact with your phone; InfoBento is just there.
artifacts.description: InfoBento has no user-facing controls. It syncs automatically via BLE, charges via solar or MagSafe passively, and refreshes on schedule. The user's only interaction is glancing at it — either on the back of their phone or standing on a counter. Configuration happens once via web UI.
artifacts.source: Core product vision — reduce screen time, not add to it. Refined in round 4: zero interaction with the device, not zero interaction period.
examples: Flip phone over to glance at display — no unlock needed
Auto-sync via BLE when mounted on phone
Solar charging when standing on counter near window
Passive MagSafe charging when collapsed on phone
No buttons anywhere on the device
counterExamples: Dedicated companion app that must be opened

artifacts.name: Pure Function Architecture
artifacts.statement: The API must be stateless — same config in, same frame buffer out, every time
artifacts.description: No server-side state, no user accounts for MVP, no databases. The cloud API is a pure function that takes a BentoConfig and returns rendered frame data. Config lives on the client (localStorage + phone).
artifacts.source: Technical constraint — edge deployability, power budget, simplicity
examples: POST /api/render takes config JSON, returns binary frame
Config stored in browser localStorage
Phone caches last frame for offline use

artifacts.name: 1-Bit Elegance
artifacts.statement: Design for the constraint — black-and-white pixels should feel intentional, not limited
artifacts.description: The eInk display is 1-bit only. Rather than fighting this constraint, embrace it. Whitespace-driven hierarchy, two font sizes (hero Spleen 8x16 + data 5x7), thin rules as dividers, differentiated box layouts per content type. Think e-paper watch faces and receipt aesthetics — dense but legible.
artifacts.source: Hardware constraint + design research (round 6). Updated after Tidbyt/Watchy/TRMNL/YotaPhone research showed whitespace > borders.
examples: Hero font for primary data (62F, 9:00, 14 days)
Thin horizontal rules as section dividers (not box borders)
Whitespace gaps between sections instead of 1px borders
High-contrast icons designed for 1-bit
counterExamples: Anti-aliased fonts that become muddy at 1-bit
1px borders around every box (old design, replaced)
More than two font sizes (creates visual noise)

artifacts.name: Free by Default
artifacts.statement: MVP box types must work without accounts, API keys, or subscriptions
artifacts.description: The five MVP box types (weather, quote, countdown, QR, text) all use free data sources or local computation. No user should need to create an account anywhere to use the basic product.
artifacts.source: User research — friction in setup kills adoption for consumer hardware
examples: Weather via Open-Meteo (no API key)
Quotes via ZenQuotes (no auth)
Countdown and QR are pure local computation
Text is user-entered
counterExamples: Requiring Google Calendar OAuth for MVP
Paid weather API with key management
Mandatory account creation before first use

artifacts.label: REQ-001
artifacts.statement: User can configure 3-6 bento boxes on the eInk display via web interface
artifacts.source: Voice spec — user wants modular customizable information boxes
artifacts.rationale: Core product value proposition — modular, personalized information display

artifacts.label: REQ-002
artifacts.statement: Device syncs display data through paired phone via BLE without requiring WiFi
artifacts.source: Voice spec — device should not be dependent on specific WiFi SSID
artifacts.rationale: Portability is key — device travels with user on phone back or in pocket, phone bridges connectivity

artifacts.label: REQ-003
artifacts.statement: Display refreshes 1-2 times per day on solar power alone under normal indoor lighting (counter-standing mode). Phone-mounted mode refreshes every few minutes via MagSafe charging.
artifacts.source: Voice spec + hardware research (issue #22). AEM10941 solar IC harvests 5-15mAh/day at 200 lux, device needs ~1mAh/day in counter mode.
artifacts.rationale: Zero-maintenance power — user should never need to charge the device manually. Dual power modes match the two physical modes.

artifacts.label: REQ-004
artifacts.statement: MVP supports 5 box types without requiring any user accounts: weather, quote, countdown, QR, text
artifacts.source: Open question resolution — free data sources prioritized for MVP
artifacts.rationale: Reduces onboarding friction to zero — unbox, configure, done

artifacts.label: REQ-005
artifacts.statement: Web UI and API served from same port in production with full HMR in development
artifacts.source: Open question resolution — same-port architecture like phasebot, Hono framework
artifacts.rationale: Simplifies deployment (single process) and dev experience (Vite HMR + API proxy)

artifacts.label: REQ-006
artifacts.statement: Config persists in browser localStorage with JSON export/import for portability
artifacts.source: Open question resolution — no server-side state for MVP
artifacts.rationale: Avoids auth complexity while keeping config portable between devices

artifacts.name: Morning glance at kitchen counter
artifacts.setting: Kitchen counter near window, 7:15 AM, making coffee before commute
artifacts.narrative: Sam's InfoBento is standing on the kitchen counter, hinged open at ~100 degrees with the solar panel aimed at the window. The P display (inner, facing the room) shows a relaxed layout: weather (62F, partly cloudy), a countdown (14 days to vacation), and a motivational quote. Sam grabs a jacket based on the weather. Before heading out, they fold the InfoBento closed and snap it onto the back of their phone via MagSafe. The D display (outer) was already showing a dense real-time layout: time, next meeting, message counts. No re-render needed — D held its frame from the last BLE sync. Total interaction with the device: zero.

Phone was in BLE range at scheduled refresh time

artifacts.title: Open Question Decisions — Rounds 1-5
artifacts.body:
Decisions made during planning sessions:

## Round 1 (resolved)
- MVP box types: weather (Open-Meteo), quote (ZenQuotes), countdown, QR, text — all free, no auth
- Web framework: Hono + Vite (same-port architecture like phasebot)
- Web app private during dev, co-hosted with tiles- and webmap.dev later
- Version starts at 0.1.0

## Round 2 (resolved)
1. MVP scope: text + countdown + weather first (proves pipeline), then QR + quote
2. Weather location: Open-Meteo geocoding API, user types city name
3. Config persistence: localStorage + JSON export/import (no server state)
4. Refresh scheduling: web UI sets schedule, phone app executes it, device responds
5. Design language: clean/minimal with sharp borders, receipt-style typography
6. Name: InfoBento (confirmed final)

## Round 3 (resolved)
1. Implementation order: text -> countdown -> weather -> QR -> quote
2. Mobile web layout: stack vertically (preview on top, config below)
3. Font: embedded small fixed-width bitmap font (5x7 or 6x8 pixel, embedded-systems style)
4. QR sizing: larger allocation — half display height or more, not constrained to a thin box
5. Name confirmed: InfoBento is final

## Round 4 — Market & Positioning (resolved 2026-04-21)
1. Primary user: Daily Glancer (the founder)
2. Distribution: Kickstarter
3. Price target: $30 (bumped from $25 after BOM analysis)
4. Hardware: ESP32-C3 + eInk + battery w/ solar drip charger + solar panel kickstand (details in issue #22)
5. Competitive positioning: resolved — 'See less. Know enough.' anti-phone angle

## Round 5 — Form Factor & Interaction Model (resolved 2026-04-21)
1. Form factor: clamshell with 180-degree hinge. Two halves: eInk display + solar panel
2. Primary mode: MagSafe-mounted on back of iPhone, eInk facing out. User flips phone to peek.
3. Secondary mode: standing on counter/desk, hinge open, solar panel aimed at window, display facing room
4. Collapsed mode: solar panel covers display, can reverse-charge via iPhone MagSafe
5. Size constraint: must fit on iPhone 15 Pro back (146.6 x 70.6mm), may partially cover camera
6. Interaction model: zero interaction with InfoBento itself. No buttons, no app to open.
7. Refresh rate: must increase in phone-mounted mode (minutes, not hours) vs standalone (1-2x/day)
8. MVP stays simple (weather, countdown, text, QR, quote). Authenticated integrations (calendar, messages, smart home) come post-MVP.
9. Kitchen counter is the hero Kickstarter scenario. Phone-mounted is the daily use case.

## Round 6 — Phase Scoping (resolved 2026-04-21)

### Phase 2 (core)
1. Add validation library (Zod or Valibot) for config schemas
2. Each box renderer handles its own data fetching/parsing — no shared data source types
3. Horizontal subdivision (side-by-side boxes) is a Phase 2 deliverable
4. Abstract display resolution so hardware change is painless

### Phase 3 (renderer)
1. CUT Floyd-Steinberg dithering — no MVP box types produce grayscale
2. 1-bit icon set for box type headers IS MVP
3. CUT frame buffer diffing — meaningless without firmware
4. QR moves up in priority (strong Kickstarter demo use case). Order: countdown -> weather -> QR -> quote
5. Hero font: Spleen 8x16 (selected over Tamzen 8x16, Tamzen 10x20, and 2x-scaled 5x7 baseline). Best balance of curve quality and vertical space. Data font stays 5x7.

### Phase 4 (API)
1. Structured error responses with field-level detail (for web UI form validation)
2. Move PNG conversion from renderer to api package
3. Health endpoint reads version from package.json (no manual bump)
4. Box-types endpoint only lists implemented/available types

### Phase 5 (web)
1. CUT Web Bluetooth — no device to pair with yet
2. Simple up/down arrow buttons for reorder (not drag-and-drop)
3. Framework: vanilla JS with reactive state pattern (selected over Preact — prototypes/svelte-editor.html preferred)
4. Client-side renderer for instant preview (no API round-trip)
5. Kickstarter MVP scope: live preview + add/remove boxes + configure text/countdown/weather + export JSON

## Still open (hardware)
- Hinge sourcing: Reell TI-C5M selected, need to order samples
- Background BLE on iOS constraints (critical for phone-mounted mode)
- eInk partial refresh strategy for D display (minute-level updates)
- BLE connection interval tuning for phone-mounted mode
- BOM at $30: dual display pushes total range to $29-50, aggressive sourcing critical

## Resolved (no longer open)
- BLE version: 5.0 (ESP32-C3 supports it natively)
- Battery capacity: ~100mAh target (352035 form factor)
- Anti-aliasing: not possible at 1-bit, solved with purpose-designed Spleen 8x16 font
- Hinge: 180-degree standard friction, book-style along 70.6mm short edge (reduced from 320-degree)
- MagSafe: full N52 ring on solar half (M-side), Qi coil inside ring
- Price: $30
- Thickness: ~8mm folded (accepted)
- Display panel: glass (not flex)
- Display resolution: 128x296 portrait
- Battery placement: solar half — avoids grip flex stress on LiPo cell. Power through hinge FPC (2 wires, ~100mA). Display half has no battery.
- Folded thickness: ~7.2mm (3.2mm display + 4.0mm solar) (standard 2.9-inch panel rotated). Codebase updated.
- Physical modes: closed (0° phone-mounted), peek (90°), counter (~100° solar charging)
- Solar charging: counter mode only, not phone-mounted

## Round 7 — Hardware Design Decisions (resolved 2026-04-21)
1. Glass eInk panel (not flex) — flex adds $7-10/unit for 0.9mm savings, not worth it at this stage
2. Accept ~8mm folded thickness — position as 'slim enough for a back pocket' (comparable to MagSafe Battery Pack at 11.3mm, thinner than most phone cases with card holders)
3. Price target bumped from $25 to $30 — BOM analysis showed charging subsystem ($13-18) + hinge ($4-30) + display ($5-8) leaves no margin at $25
4. See issue #22 for full hardware design exploration and proposed component layout

## Round 8 — Physical Modes & Hinge Hardening (2026-04-21)

### Four-surface labeling
The device has 2 halves x 2 sides = 4 distinct surfaces:
- D = eInk display face (outer face of display half)
- P = PCB face (inner face of display half — ESP32, battery)
- S = Solar panel face (outer face of solar half)
- M = MagSafe + Qi face (inner face of solar half — magnets, coil)
When closed: D faces out, M faces phone, P and S sandwiched inside.

### Three operating modes (180-degree hinge)
1. CLOSED (0°) — Phone mounted. M touches phone (MagSafe holds), D faces outward. Display visible on phone back. Solar not charging.
2. PEEK (90°) — Quick glance. Solar half flat, display half vertical. L-shape. User opens device 90° to read display while phone is on desk.
3. COUNTER (~100°) — Solar charging. M-side down as base, S faces up toward light, D faces user at angle. Standalone on counter/desk.

### Decisions
1. Peek mode is 90° (not 10-20° as originally discussed) — clear L-shape, display fully visible
2. Counter mode: solar half is the base (M-side down), solar panel faces up for charging
3. Simultaneous mount+stand is NOT a use case — device is either on phone or on counter
4. Solar charging only happens in counter mode (not phone-mounted)
5. FLAT (180°) exists mechanically but is not a useful operating mode — storage/transport only

### Dual display — DECIDED: yes, same size (Variant A)
- Two 2.9-inch 128x296 eInk panels back-to-back on display half PCB
- D (outer): real-time phone-mounted content, partial refresh every 2-5 min
- P (inner): ambient counter/peek content, full refresh 1-2x/day
- GPIO budget: 10 of 13 pins, 3 spare. Shared SPI + RST.
- Thickness: 3.2mm display half (improved from 4.4mm single-display)
- BOM: +$5-8 for second panel
- No re-render on mode switch — each display holds its own frame
- Software: extend BentoConfig with displayId: 'D' | 'P', two independent configs
- Display resolution confirmed: 128x296 portrait. Codebase updated.

artifacts.label: REQ-007
artifacts.statement: QR code box type gets a larger vertical allocation (approximately half display height) to ensure scannability
artifacts.source: Open question resolution — small QR codes in thin boxes are not scannable
artifacts.rationale: A QR code in a 35px-tall box would be too small to scan reliably. Larger allocation ensures real-world utility.

artifacts.name: Two-Font Bitmap System
artifacts.statement: Two embedded bitmap fonts — Spleen 8x16 for hero data, built-in 5x7 for labels and body text — no system font dependencies
artifacts.description: The renderer embeds two fixed-width bitmap fonts as pixel data arrays. Spleen 8x16 (purpose-designed, MIT licensed) for hero numbers and primary data (temperatures, times, countdown numbers). Built-in 5x7 for labels, secondary text, and compact data rows. Two sizes only — the contrast jump IS the visual hierarchy. No medium size.
artifacts.source: Font comparison (round 6) — Spleen 8x16 selected over Tamzen 8x16, Tamzen 10x20, and 2x-scaled 5x7 baseline. Best curve quality at minimal vertical cost.
examples: Built-in 5x7: 'WEATHER', 'Partly Cloudy', 'H:68 L:55'
Two sizes create clear hierarchy without borders
counterExamples: System fonts rendered via Canvas API
Three or more font sizes (creates visual noise)

artifacts.name: Rendering Pipeline
artifacts.description: Full rendering pipeline: config -> layout -> hero font + whitespace layout -> draw -> frame buffer. All 5 MVP box types implemented with Spleen 8x16 hero font and whitespace-based design. Dual-display support via displayId.
artifacts.scope: Core types, layout engine, embedded bitmap font, drawing primitives, text box renderer
knownLimitations: Maximum 6 boxes enforced by layout truncation
Layout engine only does vertical stacking — horizontal subdivision prototyped in preview scripts but not in core
No 1-bit icon set for box headers yet

artifacts.title: Type system allowed box type / config mismatch
artifacts.description: Original BentoBox interface used a single optional BoxConfig field, allowing { type: weather, config: { type: text } } without type error. Fixed with discriminated union (TextBentoBox | UnconfiguredBentoBox).
artifacts.evidence: Claude code review round 2, item #4 — TypeScript accepted mismatched type/config pairs
artifacts.recommendation: Maintain discriminated union pattern as new box types are added. Each box type gets its own interface pairing type with config.

artifacts.label: REQ-008
artifacts.statement: Users can see a live PNG preview of their bento layout before syncing to device
artifacts.source: Implementation need — raw binary frame buffer is not human-viewable; preview is essential for the web config experience
artifacts.rationale: Users cannot configure a display they cannot see. The first-time config scenario depends on immediate visual feedback. Phone app also needs preview before BLE sync.

artifacts.name: MagSafe Dual-Display Clamshell
artifacts.statement: InfoBento is a hinged clamshell with two eInk displays back-to-back — D (outer) for phone-mounted mode, P (inner) for counter/peek mode — connected to a solar/MagSafe half by a 180-degree hinge
artifacts.description: The device has two halves: a display half (D on outer face, P on inner face — two 2.9-inch 128x296 eInk panels back-to-back on one PCB) and a solar half (S solar panel on inner face, M MagSafe magnets on outer face). Four surfaces: D, P, S, M. Three operating modes: (1) Closed (0°) — M touches phone via MagSafe, D faces outward showing real-time data; (2) Peek (90°) — L-shape, P faces user for a quick glance; (3) Counter (~100°) — tent shape, M-side down as base, S faces up for solar charging, P faces user with ambient content. D and P are never visible simultaneously. No re-render on mode switch — each display holds its own pre-rendered frame.
artifacts.source: Rounds 5-8, dual-display exploration 2026-04-21. GPIO budget confirmed (10 of 13 pins), thickness ~7.2mm folded (3.2mm display + 4.0mm solar).
examples: Closed on phone: D shows weather, time, next event, message counts
Peek 90°: user opens device, P shows ambient quote and agenda
Counter ~100°: P shows countdown and full weather, S charges from window light
Desk flat: D readable face-up like a card, no phone needed
counterExamples: Single display that must re-render on every fold/unfold

artifacts.title: Hardware Platform
artifacts.body:
## Component Layout (dual-display, updated from issue #22)

### Display half — dual eInk back-to-back (no battery)
- D-side (outer): 2.9-inch glass eInk (79x37x1.2mm, 128x296 portrait)
- P-side (inner): 2.9-inch glass eInk (79x37x1.2mm, 128x296 portrait)
- ESP32-C3-MINI-1 (16.6x13.2x2.4mm) between panels, antenna at board edge
- PCB 0.8mm between the two panels
- NO battery — avoids grip flex stress on LiPo (users squeeze display half when holding phone)
- Half thickness: 3.2mm (1.2 + 0.8 + 1.2) — uniform, all panels full-size

### Solar half (has battery)
- M-side (outer): MagSafe magnet ring (54mm OD, 46mm ID) + Qi receiver coil
- S-side (inner): Solar panel (~70x100mm, amorphous Si, 0.22mm)
- LiPo battery GM251534 (100mAh, 15x34x2.5mm) between solar panel and MagSafe/Qi layers
- AEM10941 solar harvesting IC + MCP73831 LiPo charger
- STWLC38 or BQ51013 Qi receiver IC
- Half thickness: ~4.0mm (0.8 PCB + 2.5 battery + 0.5 solar + 0.2 margin)
- Power routed to display half through hinge FPC (2 wires, ~100mA max)
- Solar half is never squeezed — sits on surfaces or touches phone back

### GPIO allocation (13 available, 10 used)
- SPI shared: MOSI (GPIO6), SCLK (GPIO7)
- Display D: CS (GPIO10), DC (GPIO3), BUSY (GPIO1)
- Display P: CS (GPIO5), DC (GPIO4), BUSY (GPIO0)
- RST shared: GPIO9
- Battery ADC: GPIO2
- Spare: GPIO8, GPIO18, GPIO19

### Hinge
- Book-style along 70.6mm short edge
- 180-degree standard friction hinge ($1-8/unit)
- FPC through hinge: 2-4 wires (power + solar leads)

### Thickness
- Display half: 3.2mm (dual eInk back-to-back, no battery)
- Solar half: ~4.0mm (includes 2.5mm battery)
- Folded total: ~7.2mm

### BOM target: $30
- Charging subsystem: $13-18
- Hinge: $1-8 (standard friction, 180-degree)
- eInk displays x2: $10-16 (glass)
- ESP32-C3-MINI-1: $2-3
- PCB + passives: $3-5
- Total range: $29-50 (aggressive sourcing needed at low end)

artifacts.title: Market & Distribution
artifacts.body:
## Positioning
- Price target: $30 (bumped from $25 on 2026-04-21 after hardware BOM analysis)
- Distribution: Kickstarter
- Timeline: when it's ready (no fixed date)
- Primary buyer: Daily Glancer (the founder — building for himself first)

## Competitive landscape
- Phone widgets / lock screen: free, but require unlock or at minimum wake gesture
- Smartwatch complications: on wrist, always updating, but small and subscription-heavy
- Tidbyt / Vestaboard / LaMetric: $150-300, WiFi-dependent, desk-only
- DIY eInk (Waveshare, LILYGO): $15-40, no polish, requires coding

## InfoBento's gap
- Cheaper than smart displays, more polished than DIY
- Portable (phone-mounted), not desk-bound
- Solar + MagSafe = zero charging ritual
- No accounts, no subscriptions, no WiFi dependency
- The anti-phone: replaces the impulse to unlock by putting key info on the outside

## Kickstarter hero scenario
- Kitchen counter: standing up, solar panel aimed at window, morning coffee glance
- Phone-mounted daily use is the retention story, counter mode is the aspirational pitch

## Value proposition — resolved 2026-04-21
- Tagline: See less. Know enough.
- Angle: anti-gadget. Not another screen competing for attention — the screen that keeps you from reaching for one.
- $30 justification: costs less than the screen time it saves you.
- Structural moat vs Tidbyt: MagSafe phone mount. No desk display can claim 'replaces the impulse to unlock.'
- Lock screen objection: lock screen requires pick-up + wake. InfoBento works face-down on a table.
- Resolved tension: it's an 'anti-phone phone accessory' — not a desk display that also mounts to a phone.

## Kickstarter pitch (angle 1 — selected)
The problem isn't that your phone lacks information — it's that it has too much. Every unlock is a trapdoor: you check the weather and surface 20 minutes later, mid-scroll. InfoBento is a 2.9 inch eInk screen that mounts to the back of your iPhone with MagSafe. Flip your phone over. Weather, next meeting, countdown to vacation — right there, in sharp black and white, no unlock required. When you're home, stand it on the kitchen counter. The hinged solar panel aims at the window and keeps it charged indefinitely. No WiFi, no accounts, no subscriptions, no buttons. Configure your boxes once from a web page, and it just works — for months, silently, on sunlight. At $30, it costs less than the screen time it saves you. InfoBento isn't another screen competing for your attention. It's the screen that keeps you from reaching for one.

## Alternate angles (kept for reference)
- Angle 2: Your phone's off switch has a display. Clever but 'off switch' undersells — sounds like it prevents phone use rather than replaces the need for it.
- Angle 3: The last thing you check before you don't check your phone. Best closing line ('a screen you never pick up') but opener too long for tagline.

artifacts.name: Phone-back peek before unlock
artifacts.setting: Office desk, phone buzzes with a notification, mid-afternoon
artifacts.narrative: Maya's phone buzzes on the desk, screen-down. Instead of picking it up and unlocking it — which she knows will lead to 10 minutes of Slack scrolling — she glances at the D display on the back of the InfoBento. It shows: weather still 72F, next meeting in 45 min, 3 unread emails. Nothing urgent. She leaves the phone face-down and keeps working. If she wants more detail, she opens the InfoBento to 90 degrees and reads the P display — full agenda, countdown to vacation, a quote. Then she folds it back closed. No re-render, no delay. Total interaction: a glance or a flip.
preconditions: InfoBento mounted on phone back via MagSafe
Display refreshed within last few minutes via BLE
Config has weather, next event, and message count boxes
postconditions: User has ambient awareness without unlocking phone
Screen time avoided for a low-value check

artifacts.title: Display resolution mismatch: code vs hardware
artifacts.description: The codebase (DISPLAY_WIDTH=240, DISPLAY_HEIGHT=200) does not match standard 2.9-inch eInk panels which are 296x128 pixels. This needs to be reconciled once final hardware is selected. The current 240x200 dimensions may have been placeholder values. A 296x128 display is landscape-oriented and much wider than tall, which significantly affects the bento box layout strategy (horizontal subdivision becomes viable).
artifacts.recommendation: Defer resolution change until hardware is finalized, but flag that layout engine and all box renderers will need updates. Consider whether 296x128 landscape orientation changes the stacked-vertical-boxes paradigm.

artifacts.title: eInk display design research — layout patterns (addressed)
artifacts.description:
Research across Tidbyt, Watchy, TRMNL, thermal printer art, and eInk phone accessories (YotaPhone, InkCase, HiSense) yielded consistent design principles for small 1-bit displays:

1. ONE DOMINANT ELEMENT — a single large hero element (time, temperature) taking 40-50% of height reads best. Cramming too much kills legibility.
2. TWO FONT SIZES MAX — large hero + small data. No medium. The contrast jump IS the hierarchy.
3. WHITESPACE BEATS BORDERS — generous padding between sections feels cleaner than 1px borders around everything. Current renderer over-uses borders.
4. RECEIPT-STYLE LAYOUT — label left-aligned, value right-aligned, monospace. Horizontal rules as dividers.
5. 3-4 DATA ITEMS MAX — rotate screens for more info rather than crowding one frame.
6. STATIC > INTERACTIVE — eInk phone accessories that tried to be mini-Android (YotaPhone, HiSense) disappointed users. Single-purpose static frames (InkCase clock faces) worked best.
7. NO TOUCH REQUIRED — designs assuming eInk touch input universally failed. Treat the back as display-only.

The current renderer treats all boxes identically (border + uppercase label + dotted divider + wrapped text). The research points toward differentiated visual treatment per box type as the next rendering improvement.
artifacts.evidence: Web research: Tidbyt review (macwright.com), Watchy docs (sqfmi), TRMNL (trmnl.com), YotaPhone review (Engadget, Phone Scoop), InkCase (Kickstarter), thermal-sans-mono (GitHub)
artifacts.recommendation: Implement hero font size for primary data (weather temp, countdown number). Reduce border usage — use whitespace gaps instead. Differentiate box renderers visually by type. Consider screen rotation (2-3 states cycling) as an alternative to cramming 6 boxes.

artifacts.name: Web Editor Framework Comparison
artifacts.description: Two self-contained HTML prototypes comparing Preact vs vanilla JS for the web config editor. Both implement: box list with add/remove/reorder, type-specific config forms, eInk-style preview, JSON export.
artifacts.scope: Web config editor interaction model and framework evaluation
